# Workflow

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A[(survival data)] --> B[Kaplan-Meier Estimator]
  B --> C[Log Rank Test]  
  C --> D[Cox Proportional Hazards Model]
  C -.-> E[Fully parametric model]  
  C -.-> F[AFT, other exotic..]
  D --> G[Diagnostics]
  G --> D
  
  
  style D fill:#f9f
```

a. Initial displays
i. Check number of failures is sufficient for
i. For all subjects
ii. For each level of categorical variables to be included in the model
For each there should usually be a minimum of about 10, although some authors
suggest 5. If there are not sufficient for one level of a category, it may be possible to
rectify this by merging categories, but only with the guidance of a clinician. Another
option is to exclude these subjects from the analysis. If this is not possible, profile
likelihood and Bayesian methods can be used but are beyond this course. This will
also identify if any category values are not defined.
ii. Distribution of continuous predictors
The usual method is to use histograms as a graphical summary is usually easier to
interpret. What we are interested in is are there unusual values, for example zeroes
or negative values which may be used to indicate missing data, or simply values that
are so extreme that they are not biologically feasible. Skewness may indicate the
need for a transformation.
iii. Kaplan-Meier Plots

These should be performed for each categorical predictor and for continuous pre-
dictors by classifying into a small number of groups, usually 3. What is of interest

is whether there appears to be an effect of a predictor, and whether that effect is
similar over time. For continuous predictors it may also give an indication that the
effect is linear. If a numerical summary is required or useful then medians with
confidence intervals or percentage survival and confidence interval at a sensible time
are suitable.
iv. Relations (optional)
It may also be useful to investigate the relationship between the predictors. This
can be achieved through 2-way tabulation of categorical predictors, matrix scatter
plots of continuous predictors and boxplots of continuous predictors by categorical
predictors.
b. Model Building
i. Perform steps from HL&M

1. We begin by fitting a multivariable model containing all variables
significant in the univariable analysis at the 20-25 percent level,  

2. we use the p-
values from the Wald tests of the individual coefficients to identify covariates that might be deleted from the model.  

3. Following the fit of the reduced model, we assess whether removal of

the covariate has produced an "important" change in the coefficients of the vari-
ables remaining in the model. In general, we use a value of about 20 percent as an

indicator of an important change in a coefficient. If the variable excluded is an

important confounder, it should be added back into the model. This process con-
tinues until no covariates can be deleted from the model.  

4. At this point, we add to the model, one at a time, all variables ex-
cluded from the initial multivariable model to confirm that they are neither statisti-
cally significant nor an important confounder.

5. Interactions 





ii. Check proportional hazards and modify model if required
iii. Repeat until proportional hazards is OK
c. Check diagnostics for final model
i. Proportional hazards
ii. Cox-Snell
iii. dfBeta
d. Predicted survival curves
These are useful for showing the effect of predictors and the survival over time. Especially
useful with stratified models, as they show how survival differs between the strata.
e. Tabulated hazard rates

For continuous predictors this should include units. For categorical predictors the refer-
ence level should be included. Where a transformation or polynomial has been used, it

should show the variation in the effect by showing the hazard ratio at a number of values,
and for published work it may be useful to generate a plot.
